title: Marvel Product Catalogue and Product Sheets
heading_path: Marvel Product Catalogue and Product Sheets > 1 About this catalogue
citation: MCPG-01 v1.0.0, §1 About this catalogue, PDF p. 1
text:
Marvel sells 23 household cleaning SKUs in three categories: Surface Cleaners (8 SKUs), Dishwashing (7) and Laundry (8). They are sold under six brands: Marvel Clean, Marvel Pro, Marvel Bright, Marvel Fresh, Marvel Wash and Marvel Soft. 15 of the 23 SKUs are on the Must-Stock List (MSL), which means every account is expected to keep them on the shelf (see MCPG-06).

Use this catalogue to answer product questions from store owners and buyers: what a product is for, how to use it, what to be careful about, and how it performs commercially. Each product sheet has a fixed layout so the same question always finds the same answer:

- **What it is** and **How to use**: product information. This is fictional content written for the project.
- **Cautions**: safety and label points. Always defer to the printed product label (see PUB-03 for general safe-use guidance).
- **Commercial facts**: prices from the product master and performance figures from the project dataset (marked *data*). Section 5 explains how each figure is calculated.

Category value shares in the data period *(data)*: Laundry 39.6%, Surface Cleaners 32.2%, Dishwashing 28.2% of consumer sales value. MSL SKUs make up 78% of value, and the three biggest SKUs by value are Laundry Pods 42ct, Dishwasher Pods 45ct and Laundry Detergent HE 100oz.

section_title: How the commercial facts are defined
heading_path: Marvel Product Catalogue and Product Sheets > 5 Portfolio price list and definitions > 5.2 How the commercial facts are defined
citation: MCPG-01 v1.0.0, §5.2 How the commercial facts are defined, PDF p. 12
text:
- **Trade list price** is the price Marvel charges the account (retailer, chain or distributor) before any trade discount. It is the basis for all discount and margin calculations (MCPG-05).
- **Reference consumer shelf price** is the planning reference for what shoppers pay. It is 1.30 to 1.40 times the list price for every SKU. Retailers set their own shelf prices, so treat it as a reference, not a promise.
- **Marvel gross margin at list price** = (list price − unit cost) ÷ list price. Every SKU sits between 51% and 54% before discounts.
- **Consumer sales value** = units sold × the price the shopper actually paid, over reported store-days from 1 January 2025 to 31 May 2026.
- **Average units per in-stock store-day** counts only days when the store reported and the SKU did not end the day out of stock.
- **Out-of-stock rate** = reported store-SKU-days that ended with zero inventory ÷ all reported store-SKU-days. Days a store did not report are Unknown and are not counted (MCPG-08).
- **Accounts that carry it** = accounts with at least one reported sales row for the SKU. Non-MSL SKUs are carried by 124 to 141 of the 221 accounts.

title: Out-of-Stock Substitution Guide
heading_path: Out-of-Stock Substitution Guide > 1 Purpose
citation: MCPG-02 v1.0.0, §1 Purpose, PDF p. 1

title: Out-of-Stock Substitution Guide
heading_path: Out-of-Stock Substitution Guide > 2 Substitution rules
citation: MCPG-02 v1.0.0, §2 Substitution rules, PDF p. 1
text:
Offer a substitute in this order of preference:

1. **Same product, different pack size.** The same formula in a smaller or larger pack (for example Laundry Pods 20ct for Laundry Pods 42ct). This is the closest match for the shopper.
2. **Same product line, different scent or variant.** The same use and pack in another fragrance (for example Power Clean Original 1L for Power Clean Lemon 1L).
3. **Same category and use, different format.** For example HE liquid detergent instead of pods. Say clearly that the format is different.
4. **No acceptable substitute.** Some SKUs have no equivalent in the Marvel range (glass cleaner, rinse aid, stain remover, bleach). Do not force a product that does a different job; restore stock instead.

Always:

- Prefer a substitute that is **in stock in the same store today** and, when there is a choice, an **MSL** SKU.
- Stay **within the same category**. Never offer a product from another category as a substitute.
- **Never suggest combining products** to replace a missing one, and never present bleach as an alternative to a cleaner (see PUB-03).
- Do not transfer claims. A substitute does not inherit the missing product's claims (for example "antibacterial" or "with aloe").
- Show the price difference honestly. The comparisons below use the trade list price and the list price per fl oz or per count from MCPG-01.

title: Out-of-Stock Substitution Guide
section_title: Fix the cause, not only the shelf
heading_path: Out-of-Stock Substitution Guide > 8 Fix the cause, not only the shelf
citation: MCPG-02 v1.0.0, §8 Fix the cause, not only the shelf, PDF p. 5
text:
A substitution is a stop-gap. Research on shopper behaviour shows that many shoppers do not substitute at all. In one field study of real stock-outs, 41.5% went to another store and 22% postponed the purchase (PUB-01). In Marvel's own data, on days when a SKU is out of stock, its first-choice substitute sells only 2% to 4% more than usual in the same store *(data)*. So most of the lost sale is not recovered on the shelf.

To fix the cause:

- **Reorder early enough.** Orders arrive a median of 2 days after ordering for Distributors, 3 days for Modern Trade and 5 days for Traditional Trade *(data)*. An order placed when the shelf is already empty means days without stock.
- **Prioritise small accounts.** Tier 3 accounts run out of stock 15.1% of the time against 2.9% for Tier 1 *(data)*. They also tend to order when the shelf holds only about four days of sales (MCPG-04).
- **Watch MSL SKUs first.** A store fails MSL compliance for the day if even one MSL SKU is at zero (MCPG-06, MCPG-08).

title: Marvel Sales Argumentarium
heading_path: Marvel Sales Argumentarium > 1 How to use this argumentarium
citation: MCPG-03 v1.0.0, §1 How to use this argumentarium, PDF p. 1
text:
This document gives field representatives the selling stories for Marvel's categories, the degreaser line, and each channel. Every argument is built on a fact the rep can show: a price from the product master, or a figure from the project dataset (marked *data*). Use it together with the objection-handling guide (MCPG-04) and the product sheets (MCPG-01).

Three rules for every conversation:

1. **Lead with the store's own business**: availability, sales and margin on its shelf.
2. **Quote only figures you can trace** to this document or the dashboard. If a number is not here, do not invent it.
3. **Never promise an execution uplift figure.** In Marvel's data, secondary displays, planogram compliance and shelf share show at most about a 1% sales difference for the same store and SKU. That is too small to promise. Sell execution on visibility and on what the account receives in return (MCPG-05), not on a guaranteed sales increase.

text:
**What is usually behind it.** The buyer compares the trade price with a competitor's, or wants a larger discount.

**Do not.** Do not offer a discount above the cap as if it were approved, and do not quote a competitor's price.

**What is usually behind it.** Stock is sitting in the back room, or the shelf sells slowly in this store.

**Response.** Check the store's own figures in the dashboard before answering: units sold per day, stock on hand and recent invoices. If stock really is high, do not push more volume. **What is usually behind it.** The store had a recent late delivery or ran out of stock waiting for one.

**Do not.** Do not blame the store or promise a delivery date that logistics has not confirmed.

**What is usually behind it.** The buyer believes demand moves to another product on the same shelf.

**Response.** Explain that many shoppers do not substitute. They go to another store, wait, or do not buy at all, so the sale is lost for both the store and Marvel. Offer the substitution guide for emergencies, but focus on preventing the gap.

**Evidence to show.** In a field study of real stock-outs, 41.5% of shoppers went to another store, 22% postponed, 18.1% switched to another size or type, 12.2% did not buy and 6.3% switched brand (PUB-01). *(data)* In Marvel's data, the first-choice substitute sells only about 2% to 4% more on days the original is out of stock (MCPG-02). Estimated lost sales: 4.8% of potential overall, 13.8% in Tier 3 accounts.

**Do not.** Do not overstate the research: it is one field study in German and Swiss supermarkets across many categories, not Marvel's own shoppers.

title: Objection-Handling Guide
section_title: "Why should I order more often? I'm a small store."
heading_path: Objection-Handling Guide > 2 Common objections > 2.8 "Why should I order more often? I'm a small store."
citation: MCPG-04 v1.0.0, §2.8 "Why should I order more often? I'm a small store.", PDF p. 3
text:
**What is usually behind it.** Small stores have little storage, limited cash and infrequent visits.

**Response.** Agree a simple reorder point: order when the shelf still holds about a week of normal sales, not when it is empty, because delivery takes several days. Smaller, more frequent orders keep the shelf full without tying up cash.

**Evidence to show.** *(data)* Tier 3 accounts place orders when the shelf holds a median of about 4 days of sales, and 31% of their orders are placed when the shelf is already empty. As a result, 48% of Tier 3 restocks arrive after the shelf has run out, against 8% in Tier 1. Tier 3 accounts restock a SKU about every 28 days, against 12 in Tier 1 (Team 1 V3 EDA, section 8.2).

**Do not.** Do not ask a small store to hold the stock levels of a Tier 1 account.

title: Objection-Handling Guide
section_title: "Following the planogram is too much work."
heading_path: Objection-Handling Guide > 2 Common objections > 2.9 "Following the planogram is too much work."
citation: MCPG-04 v1.0.0, §2.9 "Following the planogram is too much work.", PDF p. 3
text:
**What is usually behind it.** Staff time is short, or the buyer does not see the benefit.

**Response.** Keep it practical: the planogram puts MSL SKUs where shoppers look for them and makes gaps easy to spot at a glance, which helps the store reorder in time. Offer to help reset the shelf during the visit.

**Evidence to show.** Industry evidence: a retail merchandising association study cited by Frontoni et al. (2015) linked full planogram compliance to a 7.8% sales lift and an 8.1% profit improvement (PUB-02). *(data)* Planogram compliance is 95% in Modern Trade Tier 1 accounts and 53% in Traditional Trade Tier 3 accounts.

**Do not.** Do not promise the 7.8% figure for this store. It is an industry study, and Marvel's own data shows no measurable sales difference from planogram compliance alone.

title: Objection-Handling Guide
section_title: "What do I get for giving you a secondary display?"
heading_path: Objection-Handling Guide > 2 Common objections > 2.10 "What do I get for giving you a secondary display?"
citation: MCPG-04 v1.0.0, §2.10 "What do I get for giving you a secondary display?", PDF p. 3
text:
**What is usually behind it.** The buyer wants something back for the space.

**Response.** A secondary display (endcap, island or checkout display) is one of the execution commitments that can support a larger discount under the guardrails, subject to manager review (MCPG-05). It also gives seasonal and promoted products extra visibility.

**Evidence to show.** Required trade-offs by channel and category are listed in MCPG-05, section 4. *(data)* Secondary displays are present at 49% of audited SKU visits overall: about 59% to 69% in Tier 1 accounts and 17% to 26% in Tier 3.

**Do not.** Do not promise a fixed sales increase from a display; the data does not show one.

title: Objection-Handling Guide
heading_path: Objection-Handling Guide > 2 Common objections > 2.11 "Promotions only cut my margin."
citation: MCPG-04 v1.0.0, §2.11 "Promotions only cut my margin.", PDF p. 3
text:
**What is usually behind it.** The buyer has seen promotions that moved volume but not profit.

**Response.** Show the measured effect: units go up by roughly the same percentage as the price goes down, so revenue holds while the store gains traffic and visibility. Choose the promotion type that fits the store, and stock up before it starts, because stock-outs rise on promotion days.

**Evidence to show.** *(data)* Average lift 12.9% at about 11% off; BOGO +23%, Volume +20%, TPR +15%, Feature +13%, Display +11%, Bundle +2% (MCPG-07). Stock-outs on promotion days vs other days: Modern Trade 8.3% vs 6.3%, Traditional Trade 10.4% vs 8.6%, Distributors 10.1% vs 7.7%.

**Do not.** Do not run a promotion without checking that the order will arrive before it starts.

title: Objection-Handling Guide
section_title: "(Distributor) I want the volume deal now, outside the deal period."
heading_path: Objection-Handling Guide > 2 Common objections > 2.12 "(Distributor) I want the volume deal now, outside the deal period."
citation: MCPG-04 v1.0.0, §2.12 "(Distributor) I want the volume deal now, outside the deal period.", PDF p. 4
text:
**What is usually behind it.** The distributor wants volume pricing all year.

**Response.** Volume deals are planned for set windows (Q1 and Q3). Outside them, the distributor's trade discount must stay within its guardrail cap, or go through manager review with the required commitment. Offer to plan the next order into the next volume window.

**Evidence to show.** Distributor Volume Deals: 14% off, minimum 200 units (MCPG-07). Distributor discount caps are 15.07% to 17.80% depending on category (MCPG-05).

**Do not.** Do not ask a distributor for shelf-execution commitments: distributors are wholesale accounts and negotiate volume, not shelf space.

title: Objection-Handling Guide
section_title: "Is it safe to use the degreaser or bleach with other cleaners?"
heading_path: Objection-Handling Guide > 2 Common objections > 2.13 "Is it safe to use the degreaser or bleach with other cleaners?"
citation: MCPG-04 v1.0.0, §2.13 "Is it safe to use the degreaser or bleach with other cleaners?", PDF p. 4
text:
**What is usually behind it.** A shopper or store owner asks a safety question.

**Response.** No. Never mix cleaning products. Point to the product label and the safe-use guidance: read and follow the label, ventilate, wear gloves where the label says so, and keep products away from children and pets.

**Evidence to show.** Public health guidance (CDC, PUB-03): mixing bleach with vinegar or ammonia can release chlorine or chloramine gases that can severely damage the lungs. Product cautions are in each product sheet (MCPG-01).

**Do not.** Do not give medical advice. For an exposure, direct the person to the label and to a poison control centre or medical help.

heading_path: Pricing, Discount and Commercial Guardrail Policy > 2 Price definitions
citation: MCPG-05 v1.0.0, §2 Price definitions, PDF p. 1
text:
- **Trade list price**: the price Marvel charges the account before any trade discount. It is the base for every discount and margin calculation. Prices for all 23 SKUs are in MCPG-01, section 5.1.
- **Trade discount**: the percentage taken off the list price on the invoice. In this policy, "discount" means the **total trade discount off list price** on the invoice line.
- **Net price**: what the account actually pays per unit after the trade discount.
- **Unit cost**: Marvel's cost per unit, used only to calculate margin.

- **Consumer promotion discount**: a price reduction for shoppers during a planned promotion (MCPG-07). It is separate from the trade discount and must never be added to it.

section_title: How to calculate net price and margin
heading_path: Pricing, Discount and Commercial Guardrail Policy > 3 How to calculate net price and margin
citation: MCPG-05 v1.0.0, §3 How to calculate net price and margin, PDF p. 1
text:
```text
net price      = list price x (1 - discount % / 100)
gross margin % = (net price - unit cost) / net price x 100
```

The minimum margin in the guardrails is a **gross margin on net price**, not a markup on cost.

**Worked example.** Marvel Power Clean Lemon 1L: list price $4.50, unit cost $2.10.

| Proposed discount | Net price | Gross margin |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | $4.50 | 53.3% |
| 10% | $4.05 | 48.1% |
| 12.80% (Modern Trade cap) | $3.92 | 46.5% |
| 15% | $3.82 | 45.1% |

title: Pricing, Discount and Commercial Guardrail Policy
heading_path: Pricing, Discount and Commercial Guardrail Policy > 5 How a proposal is assessed
citation: MCPG-05 v1.0.0, §5 How a proposal is assessed, PDF p. 4
text:
Every proposal gets one of three results. These are the same rules the negotiation simulator applies.

| Result | When it applies | What happens next |
|---|---|---|
| **APPROVED** | Discount is at or below the cap **and** gross margin is at or above the minimum | The representative can agree it with the account |
| **MANAGER OVERRIDE REQUIRED** | Discount is above the cap, gross margin is still at or above the minimum, **and** the account commits to the required execution trade-off | Prepare the proposal with the evidence for regional manager review (MCPG-09). Do not confirm it to the account yet |
| **POLICY BREACH / REJECTED** | Gross margin falls below the minimum, **or** the discount is above the cap without the required commitment | Do not offer it. Explain the limit and propose an alternative within policy |

**Examples** (Marvel Power Clean Lemon 1L, Modern Trade, Surface Cleaners: cap 12.80%, minimum margin 26.62%):

- 10% discount: margin 48.1%, within the cap → **APPROVED**.
- 15% discount, account commits to +10 percentage points of shelf share or one secondary display: above the cap, margin 45.1% is above the floor → **MANAGER OVERRIDE REQUIRED**.
- 15% discount, no commitment → **POLICY BREACH / REJECTED**.

title: Pricing, Discount and Commercial Guardrail Policy
heading_path: Pricing, Discount and Commercial Guardrail Policy > 6 Execution commitments (trade-offs)
citation: MCPG-05 v1.0.0, §6 Execution commitments (trade-offs), PDF p. 4
text:
The guardrails name the commitment an account must make for a discount above the cap:

- **"+10% / +15% shelf share"** means **percentage points**, not a relative increase: if the current share is 30%, +15% means 45%, not 34.5%.
- **"Secondary display" and "featured endcap"** are the same thing. Any off-shelf placement counts: an endcap, a free-standing island or a checkout display.
- **"Featured endcap placement for 4 weeks"** means the display stays in place for four consecutive weeks.
- **"100% MSL compliance + planogram adherence"** means every Must-Stock SKU is on the shelf and placed according to the planogram (MCPG-06).

A commitment must be verifiable from a later field audit (planogram compliance, shelf share and secondary display are all recorded in execution audits). Record the date of the latest audit with the proposal.

citation: MCPG-06 v1.0.0, §5 Shelf share, PDF p. 2
text:
**Shelf share** (`shelf_share_pct`) is recorded at each audit for each audited SKU. In the current audit data it is the **allocation of shelf space among the Marvel SKUs audited in that category during the visit**: the shares of the SKUs in one category visit add up to 100%. A SKU's share is therefore roughly 100 divided by the number of SKUs audited (about 14.6% on average).

How to read it:

- Use it to compare how space is split between Marvel SKUs, for example whether the degreaser gets a fair share of the Surface Cleaners space.
- It is **not** Marvel's share of the whole category shelf against competitors. The data has no competitor information.
- Compare shelf share only between visits with a similar number of audited SKUs.

section_title: Promotion types and the sales lift each delivers
heading_path: Trade Promotions Guide and 2025-2026 Promotion Calendar > 2 Promotion types and the sales lift each delivers
citation: MCPG-07 v1.0.0, §2 Promotion types and the sales lift each delivers, PDF p. 1
text:
**BOGO promotions give the biggest sales lift (+23% units), followed by Distributor Volume deals (+20%) and TPRs (+15%). Bundles add almost nothing (+2%).**

*(data)* "Extra units" compares, for the same store and SKU in the same month, average daily units on promotion days with non-promotion days, using in-stock days only. The implied elasticity is the percentage change in units divided by the percentage change in price.

| Type | What it is | Average discount | Extra units vs normal days *(data)* | Implied price elasticity *(data)* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BOGO | Buy One Get One: a multi-buy mechanic. In the calendar it is valued as a discount percentage. | 15% | +23% | -1.29 |
| Volume | Distributor volume deal: a discount for orders above a minimum quantity. | 14% | +20% | -1.20 |
| TPR | Temporary Price Reduction: a straight price cut for a fixed period. | 10% | +15% | -1.27 |
| Feature | The product is featured in the retailer's advertising (flyer, digital or in-store media) at a reduced price. | 8% | +13% | -1.38 |
| Display | The promoted product gets an off-shelf display (endcap, island) together with a price reduction. | 9% | +11% | -1.18 |
| Bundle | Products sold together as a bundle at a combined price, for example around the holidays. | 12% | +2% | -0.18 |

Across all promotions, a store-SKU sold **12.9% more units at an average discount of 11%**, an elasticity of about **-1.0**: units rise by roughly the same percentage as the price falls. By channel *(data)*: Modern Trade +12.2% (elasticity -1.02), Traditional Trade +11.0% (-0.96), Distributors +19.9% (-1.20). By category: Surface Cleaners +12.6%, Dishwashing +11.7%, Laundry +15.2%.

1. **Order early.** Stock-outs are more frequent on promotion days *(data)*: Modern Trade 8.3% vs 6.3% on other days, Traditional Trade 10.4% vs 8.6%, Distributors 10.1% vs 7.7%. 3. **Check MSL first.** A promotion on a category does not help if an MSL SKU in that category is out of stock.
4. **Watch the end.** After a deep promotion, the store may hold extra stock; adjust the next order instead of pushing more volume.

title: Commercial KPI Handbook
heading_path: Commercial KPI Handbook > 3 The five KPIs > 3.3 Sell-in vs Sell-out Gap %
citation: MCPG-08 v1.0.0, §3.3 Sell-in vs Sell-out Gap %, PDF p. 2
text:
- **Definition:** (sell-in units - sell-out units) / sell-out units x 100, with **both sides over the same time window**. A positive gap means Marvel shipped more than shoppers bought (risk of stock building up); a negative gap means less (risk of stock-outs).
- **Time alignment:** each sell-in invoice is dated on a Monday and covers the sell-out week that ended the day before. Traditional Trade accounts are invoiced about every two weeks, so compare over matching two-week or monthly windows. A store-SKU-week without an invoice counts as zero sell-in once the invoice data for that period is complete.
- **Platform metric:** `sell_in_out_gap` = comparable gap units / comparable sell-out units, using an identical period, view and alignment.
- **Baseline** *(data, Team 1 V3 EDA section 7)*: Modern Trade +11.4%, Distributors +11.3%, Traditional Trade -44.9%, all accounts -2.1%. The all-account figure hides two opposite patterns, so always show the gap by channel.

section_title: OOS risk prediction and visit ranking
heading_path: Commercial KPI Handbook > 5 OOS risk prediction and visit ranking
citation: MCPG-08 v1.0.0, §5 OOS risk prediction and visit ranking, PDF p. 2
text:
- **What is predicted:** whether a store-SKU will be out of stock on **any** of the next 7 days after the scoring date.
- **Minimum quality, fixed:** precision of at least 0.75, recall of at least 0.70 and ROC-AUC of at least 0.80. These thresholds cannot be lowered.
- **Visit ranking:** stores are ranked by the potential lost net sales at risk (units at risk x list price), giving priority to the highest OOS risk and the largest MSL gaps.
- **Until a model is released**, predictions and rankings are **unavailable**. The copilot must say "not available", never "0% risk".

title: Regional Manager Guide: Deal Review, Escalation and Exception Management
section_title: Reviewing a MANAGER OVERRIDE REQUIRED proposal
heading_path: Regional Manager Guide: Deal Review, Escalation and Exception Management > 2 Reviewing a MANAGER OVERRIDE REQUIRED proposal
citation: MCPG-09 v1.0.0, §2 Reviewing a MANAGER OVERRIDE REQUIRED proposal, PDF p. 1
text:
A proposal reaches you when the discount is above the account's cap, the gross margin is still at or above the minimum, and the account has offered the required execution commitment. Check, in this order:

1. **Margin.** Recalculate the gross margin on net price with the reference list price and unit cost (MCPG-05, section 3). If it is below the minimum, it is not an override case; it is a policy breach.
2. **The commitment matches the guardrail.** The commitment must be the one named for the channel and category (for example "+15% shelf share or 1 secondary display" for Modern Trade Laundry). "+15%" means 15 percentage points.
3. **The commitment can be verified.** Note the date of the latest audit for the store and SKU and what it showed (planogram, shelf share, secondary display). Agree when the next audit will confirm the commitment. Old audit evidence is not proof of current execution.
4. **Account context.** Look at the account's recent trade discount (28-day weighted), its stock position and its sell-in vs sell-out gap. Do not approve deeper discounts for an account that is already over-shipped.
5. **Record the decision** with the scenario's data version, date, inputs and outcome. A saved scenario is a record of the decision, not an approval in the shared data.

**Past invoices are not precedent.** Some historical invoices carry a source flag for exceeding a limit, and some exceed the cap without a flag. Treat these flags as history about that invoice, not as approval or rejection of a new proposal.

section_title: The five ways shoppers respond to an out-of-stock
heading_path: Shopper Responses to Retail Out-of-Stocks (Public Research Summary) > 2 The five ways shoppers respond to an out-of-stock
citation: PUB-01 v1.0.0, §2 The five ways shoppers respond to an out-of-stock, PDF p. 1
text:
Research on out-of-stocks groups shopper reactions into five types (as described by Helm and Hegenbart):

1. **Item switch:** buying the same brand in another size, pack or variant.
2. **Brand switch:** buying another brand in the same category.
3. **Store switch:** buying the product in another store on the same day.
4. **Postponement:** buying the product on the next regular shopping trip.
5. **Cancellation:** not buying at all, or not for a long time.

Only the first response keeps the sale for the manufacturer. For the retailer, item and brand switches keep the sale in the store, while store switches and cancellations lose it.

title: Shopper Responses to Retail Out-of-Stocks (Public Research Summary)
section_title: What a field study of real stock-outs found
heading_path: Shopper Responses to Retail Out-of-Stocks (Public Research Summary) > 3 What a field study of real stock-outs found
citation: PUB-01 v1.0.0, §3 What a field study of real stock-outs found, PDF p. 1
text:
Helm and Hegenbart interviewed shoppers at the checkouts of supermarkets in three retail chains in Germany and Switzerland, right after shoppers had actually met an empty shelf. 205 usable interviews covered 18 product categories, including household products (15.1% of cases).

- **Responses:** store switch 41.5%, postponement 22%, item switch (other size or type) 18.1%, cancellation 12.2%, brand switch 6.3%.
- **Frequency:** about one in ten shoppers reported not finding a product they wanted.
- **Real vs hypothetical:** earlier studies, mostly hypothetical ("what would you do if..."), found more substitution. Real stock-outs produced more store switching and cancellation, so hypothetical surveys may understate the damage.
- **What drives the response:** the availability of an **acceptable alternative product** and **store loyalty** had the biggest effects. Offering acceptable alternatives reduced store switching and cancellation. Loyal shoppers were less likely to switch stores after a one-off stock-out.
- **Timing:** urgency and shopping time mattered. The authors point to empty shelves at the end of the week as a known problem and recommend that retailers, manufacturers and logistics partners secure availability on critical days.

The paper also summarises earlier studies. In a 2002 meta-analysis by Gruen, Corsten and Bharadwaj, as reported in Helm and Hegenbart's Table 1, the average responses were: item switch 19%, brand switch 26%, store switch 31%, postponement 15% and cancellation 9%. Helm and Hegenbart also cite estimates that stock-outs cause average sales losses of up to about 4%.

text:
The report recommends communicating these safe practices:
